questions.q: Write the augmented matrix for the system $2x+y-z=3$, $x-3y+2z=-1$, $4x+y+z=5$.
questions.answer: $\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}2&1&-1&3\\1&-3&2&-1\\4&1&1&5\end{array}\right]$.

questions.q: List the three types of elementary row operations.
questions.answer: 1. Swap two rows. 2. Multiply a row by a nonzero scalar. 3. Add a multiple of one row to another row.
From the second equation, $x=1+y$. Substituting: $2(1+y)+3y=7 \Rightarrow 5y=5 \Rightarrow y=1$, so $x=2$. Solution: $(2,1)$.
From the second equation, $y=11-5x$. Substituting: $3x-2(11-5x)=4 \Rightarrow 13x=26 \Rightarrow x=2$, so $y=1$. Solution: $(2,1)$.

From the first equation, $x=6-y-z$. Substituting into the third: $2(6-y-z)+5y-z=27 \Rightarrow 3y-3z=15 \Rightarrow y=5+z$. Substituting into the second: $2(5+z)+5z=-4 \Rightarrow 7z=-14 \Rightarrow z=-2$, so $y=3$ and $x=6-3-(-2)=5$. Solution: $(5,3,-2)$.

sections.heading: Why row operations preserve the solution set

questions.q: Explain briefly why multiplying a row by a nonzero constant $c$ doesn't change a system's solution set.
questions.answer: Multiplying both sides of an equation by a nonzero $c$ produces an equivalent equation, since the operation is invertible — dividing by $c$ recovers the original equation exactly.

questions.q: Why is the restriction $c\ne0$ needed for this row operation?
questions.answer: If $c=0$, the row becomes the zero row, which is not invertible — the original row's information is destroyed, so the resulting system need not have the same solution set as the original.
Adding the equations: $6x=12 \Rightarrow x=2$. From the second: $y=2x-2=2$. Solution: $(2,2)$.
From the first: $x=5-2y$. Substituting: $3(5-2y)-y=1 \Rightarrow 15-7y=1 \Rightarrow y=2$, $x=1$. Solution: $(1,2)$.

From the first: $y=5-2x-z$. Substituting into the second: $x-(5-2x-z)+2z=1 \Rightarrow 3x+3z=6 \Rightarrow x=2-z$. Substituting into the third: $3(2-z)+2(5-2(2-z)-z)-z=8 \Rightarrow 8-2z=8 \Rightarrow z=0$. Then $x=2$, $y=1$. Solution: $(2,1,0)$.

sections.heading: Systems with no solution or infinitely many solutions

questions.q: Solve $x+y=3$, $2x+2y=8$, and explain what you find.
questions.answer: The second equation simplifies to $x+y=4$, which contradicts $x+y=3$. No values satisfy both — the system is inconsistent (no solution); the two lines are parallel and distinct.

questions.q: Solve $x-y=1$, $2x-2y=2$, and explain what you find.
questions.answer: The second equation is exactly $2\times$ the first, so every solution of the first automatically satisfies the second — infinitely many solutions, $x=1+t$, $y=t$ for any $t$. The two equations describe the same line.

sections.heading: Setting up a system from a word problem

questions.q: A store sells adult tickets for 8 dollars and child tickets for 5 dollars. On a day when 90 tickets were sold for 600 dollars total, set up a system of equations for the number of adult ($a$) and child ($c$) tickets sold.
Solve the system from the previous question.
questions.answer: From the first equation, $c=90-a$. Substituting: $8a+5(90-a)=600 \Rightarrow 3a=150 \Rightarrow a=50$, $c=40$. Solution: 50 adult tickets, 40 child tickets.

sections.heading: Reading a solution from row echelon form

questions.q: The augmented matrix $\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&0&0&3\\0&1&0&-2\\0&0&1&5\end{array}\right]$ is already in reduced row echelon form. State the solution.
questions.answer: Each row reads directly as a solved variable: $x=3$, $y=-2$, $z=5$.

questions.q: Verify that $(x,y,z)=(1,2,-1)$ solves $x+y+z=2$, $2x-y+z=-1$, $x+2y-3z=8$.
For which value of $k$ does $x+2y=3$, $3x+ky=9$ have infinitely many solutions?
questions.answer: Scaling the first equation by $3$ gives $3x+6y=9$, which is identical to the second equation exactly when $k=6$ — then the two equations describe the same line, giving infinitely many solutions.

questions.q: A system of two linear equations in $x,y$ is consistent if it has at least one solution. Geometrically, what does an inconsistent system of two lines look like?
questions.answer: Two parallel, distinct lines — same slope, different intercepts — so they never meet and the system has no solution.

questions.q: Is the system $2x-y=3$, $4x-2y=7$ consistent?
questions.answer: Scaling the first equation by $2$ gives $4x-2y=6$, which contradicts $4x-2y=7$. The system is inconsistent (no solution).

sections.heading: Number of solutions from row echelon form

questions.q: A row echelon form has a row $\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}0&0&0&5\end{array}\right]$. What does this tell you about the system?
questions.answer: This row reads $0=5$, a contradiction — the system has no solution (it's inconsistent), regardless of what the other rows say.

questions.q: A $3\times3$ system row-reduces to a row echelon form with a row of all zeros (no contradiction) and only 2 nonzero pivot rows. What does this tell you?
questions.answer: There are only 2 independent equations for 3 unknowns, so one variable is free — the system has infinitely many solutions.

questions.q: Solve by back-substitution: $x+2y-z=4$, $y+3z=5$, $2z=6$.
questions.answer: From the third equation, $z=3$. Substituting into the second: $y+9=5 \Rightarrow y=-4$. Substituting into the first: $x+2(-4)-3=4 \Rightarrow x=15$. Solution: $(15,-4,3)$.

questions.q: A system is homogeneous if every equation equals $0$ (e.g. $2x-y=0$, $x+3y=0$). Explain why $x=y=0$ is always a solution of a homogeneous system.
questions.answer: Substituting $x=y=0$ makes every left-hand side (a sum of terms each with a variable factor) equal to $0$, matching the right-hand side — this "trivial solution" always works, whatever the coefficients are.

questions.q: Solve the homogeneous system $2x-y=0$, $x+3y=0$.
questions.answer: From the first, $y=2x$. Substituting into the second: $x+3(2x)=0 \Rightarrow 7x=0 \Rightarrow x=0$, so $y=0$. Only the trivial solution $(0,0)$.
